title: The Slow Undertow
premise: Xanthe Montrose, a former court stenographer who fled a wrongful conviction he helped manufacture, lives quietly in a coastal town, writing postcards to an address that burned down years ago—penance he can never send. When Emeric Vasseur, the last fluent speaker of a dying local language, asks Xanthe to become his final student, the lessons force him to translate not just words but the testimony he once falsified. As Emeric's health fails and a journalist begins sniffing around the old case, Xanthe must choose between his perfected invisibility and public confession. In the end, he testifies—not to save himself, but to free the man he wronged—and records Emeric's language in full on the night Emeric dies, finding that justice and memory are the same act of speaking what everyone else has agreed to forget.
about_author: Hazel Ishikawa is a former legal transcriptionist who spent a decade documenting courtrooms before turning to fiction. She writes from a small island town where she volunteers teaching endangered-language preservation workshops.

chapters.title: The Address That Burned
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. We meet him writing postcards to 14 Alder Row, an address destroyed in a fire years ago, and perfecting the smile that ends conversations at the post office. The emotional beat is controlled loneliness—the ritual of penance without absolution.

chapters.title: A Man Who Speaks Alone
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the library he encounters Emeric Vasseur, an old fisherman muttering in an unrecognizable tongue, correcting the dictionary of a dead language no one wants. Emeric recognizes something guarded in Xanthe and asks, bluntly, for one final student. Beat: reluctant curiosity cracking routine.

chapters.title: First Lessons
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Xanthe and Emeric. Early lessons in Emeric's kitchen: words for tide, debt, forgiveness—distinctions English collapses. Emeric teaches that the language has no word for 'innocent,' only 'not yet accused.' Xanthe flinches. Beat: the past pressing through vocabulary.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Emeric's POV. Emeric shows Xanthe old photographs of the town, including one with a young court clerk whose face Xanthe pretends not to know—his own. Emeric reveals he knew the convicted man, Tomas Reyes, and believes him innocent. Beat: dread disguised as nostalgia.

chapters.title: What the Record Says
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV in flashback interwoven with present. We learn Xanthe falsified or omitted testimony under pressure from Judge Harrow, burying evidence that would have freed Reyes. His postcards are addressed to the burned house where the exculpatory witness once lived. Beat: shame surfacing.

chapters.title: The Journalist
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Dana Okafor, an investigative reporter reopening the Reyes case, arrives in town asking about the original transcript. Xanthe's smile finally fails; she notices. Meanwhile Emeric's health declines sharply. Beat: tightening vise—exposure from outside, mortality from within.

chapters.title: Words for What Cannot Be Unsaid
chapters.summary: Emeric's POV. Too weak to teach standing, Emeric dictates the language's mourning songs and its formal confession rite—a structure requiring the speaker to name every person harmed. He tells Xanthe he has known who he was since the first lesson. Beat: confrontation as compassion.

chapters.title: The Rite
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In Emeric's kitchen, Xanthe performs the confession rite aloud in the dying language, naming Reyes, the burned house, the judge, himself. Dana, tipped by Emeric, listens from the doorway. Beat: catharsis—the smile abandoned entirely.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Xanthe gives a sworn statement to Dana and the district attorney, surrendering his anonymity and accepting prosecution risk. Reyes's conviction is moved toward vacatur. Emeric, hospitalized, hears the news and speaks a word Xanthe now understands: 'enough.' Beat: justice outside the law achieved inside it.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. On Emeric's final night, they record the complete lexicon together, Xanthe transcribing as he once did in court—but this time faithfully. After Emeric dies, Xanthe mails one last postcard to 14 Alder Row, then stops writing them. Beat: quiet resolution—memory kept, guilt released, voice found.
